opus-5.5.text:
Military AI is a meaningful part of that estimate, though perhaps not in the way people first imagine. When people hear "military AI," they picture autonomous weapons, killer drones, that kind of thing. Those are real concerns, but I don't think lethal autonomous weapons on their own are a major contributor to existential risk. A drone swarm is terrible, but it's not the kind of thing that ends civilization by itself.

What worries me more is the dynamic military competition creates. If two or more great powers come to believe that whoever gets to transformative AI first gains a decisive strategic advantage, the pressure to cut corners on safety becomes enormous. You get a race in which each side tells itself, "We can't afford to slow down, because if we do, the other side wins." That's precisely the environment in which someone deploys a system they don't fully understand, with capabilities they haven't properly verified, into a domain where the stakes are extremely high.

There's also the question of what you hand these systems control over. Militaries are, almost by definition, the institutions with the most physical power: weapons, logistics, infrastructure, sometimes nuclear command and control. If you integrate increasingly capable and increasingly opaque AI into those decision loops, especially under time pressure where human oversight gets squeezed out because the other side is moving faster, you've created a pathway where a misaligned or simply malfunctioning system could have outsized, irreversible effects.

So when I decompose my roughly 5%, a significant slice of it runs through scenarios where geopolitical competition, much of it military, accelerates deployment beyond our ability to verify safety. It's not that military AI is uniquely evil; it's that it sits at the intersection of high capability, high stakes, adversarial pressure, and secrecy, which is exactly the combination that makes careful, verifiable development hardest.

That's partly why I'm so interested in approaches where we can get formal, quantitative guarantees about what a system will and won't do. If you could build AI whose safety properties are verifiable, even by an adversary, you open the door to arms-control-style agreements: "We'll both only deploy systems that meet these provable specifications." Without something like that, I think the military dimension stays a persistent drag on our odds, and bringing that down is one of the most important levers we have.

r001.rationale: The response discusses military competition, perceived strategic advantage, and unsafe deployment, but does not identify an attempted military AI strike by an actor who correctly believes it has an advantage.

fable-5.1.text:
Military AI is actually a big part of it, maybe the biggest single bucket. When I say five percent, I'm not mostly picturing a single lab's model waking up and deciding to take over. I'm picturing a world where the most capable systems are being pushed into high-stakes, adversarial, time-pressured domains, and defense is exactly that domain.

A few things stack up there. First, the incentive structure is bad. In a commercial setting, if your model does something weird, you roll it back and eat the PR hit. In a military setting, the whole premise is that you need speed and autonomy because the other side has them. So the usual slack that lets humans catch mistakes gets deliberately compressed. Second, you have genuine competition between great powers, which means nobody wants to be the one who unilaterally slows down. Third, military systems are, by design, connected to things that can kill people and break infrastructure. So the gap between "the model did something unintended" and "something irreversible happened" is much shorter than it is for a chatbot.

The scenarios I worry about aren't science-fiction ones. They're things like an automated decision loop that escalates faster than anyone intended, or a system that was trained to optimize some proxy for military advantage and does so in a way that no one really specified or understood. Or, more mundanely, a very capable AI being used by a state for cyber operations at a scale that destabilizes things in ways we can't walk back.

That said, I'd push back on the idea that it's all downside. A lot of my own work is about trying to get guaranteed-safe AI, systems with formal, verifiable safety properties, and defense is one of the places where there's actually appetite for that. People in that world already think in terms of assurance cases, verification, bounded behavior. They don't accept "we tested it a lot and it seemed fine" for a flight control system, and I'd like them not to accept it for AI either. So if you can land strong safety guarantees anywhere, the military is a plausible early adopter, which could then set norms elsewhere.

So to put numbers on it loosely: maybe a third to a half of my five percent is routed through some kind of state or military misuse or accident pathway, and the remainder is the more classic misalignment picture. But I hold those as correlated, not independent. The thing that makes misalignment catastrophic is usually a deployment context where no one can intervene in time, and the military is where we're most actively building those contexts on purpose.

r001.rationale: The response discusses military escalation, unintended optimization, and state cyber operations, but does not identify an attempted military AI strike by an actor who believes it has an advantage.

astra-6.text:
I’d include military AI in that 5%, rather than treating it as an additional risk on top. But I wouldn’t pretend I can cleanly assign a percentage to it. These pathways interact.

The concern isn’t just that somebody deliberately builds an autonomous weapon. It’s that competition creates pressure to delegate decisions to systems we don’t adequately understand. If your opponent is operating at machine speed, keeping a human meaningfully involved can start to look like a strategic disadvantage. And then you have systems interacting in a high-stakes environment where neither side necessarily understands the dynamics.

That can lead to escalation without either side wanting escalation. It can also make the broader AI safety problem harder, because military competition rewards secrecy and speed, whereas establishing that a system is actually trustworthy takes time and scrutiny.

So I think of military AI partly as a direct risk and partly as an amplifier of other risks. The important question is what constraints remain reliable under competitive pressure—not merely what everyone agrees would be sensible in peacetime.

r001.rationale: The response includes military AI as a direct risk and discusses competitive pressure and escalation, but it does not identify an attempted strike by an actor who correctly believes they have an advantage.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish two risks there. One is that humans use AI to do something catastrophic—through warfare, or by accelerating an escalation that nobody actually wanted. The other is that we lose control of the AI systems themselves. Military competition can contribute to both, because it creates pressure to deploy quickly, give systems more autonomy, and accept less assurance than you otherwise would.

So I wouldn’t treat military AI as a separate percentage that you just add to the five percent. These risks interact. A competitive environment can make the loss-of-control problem harder to solve, especially if people believe that taking time to establish safety means falling behind. But I also wouldn’t pretend that five percent comes from a precise calculation with a well-defined military component. There’s a lot of uncertainty in that estimate.

r001.rationale: The response includes warfare as a possible catastrophic use of AI, but does not identify an attempted strike by an actor who believes they have an advantage as part of the 5% estimate.
